name: מכפלה סקלרית, נורמה, זווית והטלה – הסבר ותרגול (באנגלית)

functions.name: texp
functions.body: if numberp(x) and x<0 then concat("\\left(",tex1(x),"\\right)") else tex1(x)

functions.name: texsumf
functions.body: block([L:first(args(e))], concat(tex1(first(L)), apply(sconcat, map(lambda([t], concat("+",texp(t))), rest(L)))))

functions.name: texnsum
functions.body: block([L:first(args(e))], concat(tex1(first(L)), apply(sconcat, map(lambda([t], if numberp(t) and t<0 then concat("-",tex1(-t)) else concat("+",tex1(t))), rest(L)))))

functions.name: cft
functions.body: concat(if c<0 then "-" else (if fst then "" else "+"), if abs(c)=1 then "" else tex1(abs(c)), tex1(s))

functions.name: texlin
functions.body: block([L:args(e), out:"", f:true], for k:1 thru length(L) step 2 do (if L[k]#0 then (out:concat(out, cft(L[k],L[k+1],f)), f:false)), if out="" then "0" else out)

questiontext:
The scalar product of two vectors in \(R^3\) is given by

\[{{CT:0}} \cdot {{CT:1}} = {{CT:2}}\]

Let us review the basic properties of scalar properties:

  1. Linearity: \( (av+bu) \cdot w = a v \cdot w + b u \cdot w, \quad \forall a,b \in R, u,v,w \in R^3 \)
  2. Symmetry: \( v \cdot w = w \cdot v, \quad \forall v,w \in R^3\)
  3. Positivity: \(v \cdot v \ge 0 \) with equality holding if and only if \(v = 0\) is the zero vector.

The scalar product immediately enables us to calculate a few geometric properties:

  • Length of a vector: \(||v|| = \sqrt{v \cdot v}\). This is also referred to as the norm of the vector \(v\). The positivity axiom assures that the number within the square root is always non-negative.
  • The angle \(\phi\) between two vectors \(v,w \in R^n\) is given by: \( \cos(\phi) = \frac{v \cdot w}{||v|| ||w||}\). The fact that the number on the right of the equation is in \([-1,1]\) and therefore is indeed a cosine of an angle is known as the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality.
  • The projection of the vector \(w\) on the linear subspace \(Span(v)\) is given by:

    \[Pr_{span(v)}(w) = \frac{w \cdot v}{v \cdot v} v\]

    Note that this projection is a vector, which is a scalar multiple of \(v\).

Let us make sure we understand how to carry out these calculations with the vectors:

\[v = {{CT:3}}, w = {{CT:4}}.\]

Calculate:

a

The inner product

\(v \cdot w =\) [[input:ans1]]
[[validation:ans1]]
b

The norm

\(||v|| =\) [[input:ans2]]
[[validation:ans2]]
c

The cosine of the angle \(\phi\) between these two vectors

\(\cos(\phi) =\) [[input:ans3]]
[[validation:ans3]]
d

The projection

\(Pr_{span(v)}(w) =\) [[input:ans4]]
[[validation:ans4]]

How to enter: each entry in its own box: a number, a fraction (e.g. 1/2) or an expression (e.g. sqrt(2)).
generalfeedback:
Outline: All four quantities are built from scalar products: compute \(v\cdot w\) and \(v\cdot v\), \(w\cdot w\) once, then use the formulas for the norm, the cosine of the angle and the projection.
Step 1 — The inner product (part a)
Multiply corresponding components and add:

\[ v\cdot w={{CT:5}}={{CT:6}}={{CT:7}} \]

Step 2 — The norm (part b)
By definition \(||v||=\sqrt{v\cdot v}\), the square root of the sum of the squares of the components:

\[ ||v||=\sqrt{{{CT:8}}}=\sqrt{ {{CT:9}} } \]

[[if test="{{CT:18}}"]]Hence

\[ ||v||={{CT:10}} \]

[[elif test="{{CT:19}}"]]Taking the square factor out of the root:

\[ ||v||=\sqrt{ {{CT:11}}\cdot {{CT:12}} }={{CT:10}}\sqrt{ {{CT:12}} } \]

[[/if]]
Step 3 — The cosine of the angle (part c)
For the formula we also need the norm of \(w\):

\[ ||w||=\sqrt{{{CT:13}}}=\sqrt{ {{CT:14}} }. \]

Then

\[ \cos(\phi) = \frac{v \cdot w}{||v|| ||w||}=\frac{ {{CT:7}} }{\sqrt{ {{CT:9}} }\,\sqrt{ {{CT:14}} }}={{CT:15}} \]

[[if test="{{CT:20}}"]]The scalar product is 0, so the vectors are orthogonal and the angle between them is a right angle.[[/if]]
Step 4 — The projection (part d)
The coefficient of \(v\) in the projection is the scalar \(\frac{w\cdot v}{v\cdot v}\), with the values computed above:

\[ \frac{w \cdot v}{v \cdot v}=\frac{ {{CT:7}} }{ {{CT:9}} }={{CT:16}} \]

Multiplying the vector by this scalar (each entry separately):

\[ Pr_{span(v)}(w) = {{CT:16}}{{CT:3}} = {{CT:17}} \]

on_true.feedback: Part a — correct. Your scalar product is correct.

on_false.feedback:
Part a — incorrect. You made a mistake calculating the scalar product. The correct calculation is:

\[{{CT:3}}.{{CT:4}} = {@a1@} = {{CT:7}}\]

on_true.feedback: Part b — correct. The calculation of the norm \(||v||\) is correct.
Part b — incorrect. It appears that you forgot the square root in the calculation \(||v||=\sqrt{v\cdot v}\).

on_false.feedback:
Part b — incorrect. You made a mistake calculating the norm. The correct calculation is:

\[\left|\left| {{CT:3}} \right|\right| = {@a2@} = {{CT:21}}\]

on_true.feedback: Part c — correct. Your calculation for \(\cos(\phi)\) is correct.

on_false.feedback: Part c — incorrect. Your calculation for \(cos(\phi)\) is wrong. Remember the formula is \( \cos(\phi) = \frac{v \cdot w}{||v|| ||w||}\).

on_true.feedback: Part d — correct. Your calculation for the projection is correct.

on_false.feedback:
Part d — incorrect. Something is wrong with the way you calculated the projection. Recall the formula:

\[Pr_{span(v)}(w) = \frac{w \cdot v}{v \cdot v} v\]

In our case:

\[ \frac{w \cdot v}{v \cdot v} = {@scal@}, v = {{CT:3}}\]

Multiplying the vector by the scalar (each entry separately) yields:

\[Pr_{span(v)}(w) = \frac{w \cdot v}{v \cdot v} v = {{CT:17}}\]
